results.name: above_vs_below_range
results.description: Yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the largest example minus yes-rate for targets 1-20 below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward (toward larger numbers) more than the model, below null means they extend downward more.

results.name: within_set_target_discrimination
results.description: Trial-weighted mean, over number_sets with >=40 trials, of the variance across targets of the per-target yes-rate; observed below null means the model discriminates between targets of the same set more sharply than people (people's generalisation flatter), above null means people discriminate targets more sharply than the model.
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_discrimination
# description: Trial-weighted mean, over number_sets with >=40 trials, of the variance across targets of the per-target yes-rate; observed below null means the model discriminates between targets of the same set more sharply than people (people's generalisation flatter), above null means people discriminate targets more sharply than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    pt_ = df.groupby([s, df["target"].astype(int)])["rating"].mean()
    v = pt_.groupby(level=0).var(ddof=0)
    n = s.value_counts()
    keep = n[n >= 40].index.intersection(v.index)
    if len(keep) == 0:
        return 0.0
    w = n[keep].to_numpy().astype(float)
    return float(np.sum(v[keep].to_numpy() * w) / w.sum())

results.name: outlier_majority_parity_effect
results.description: For sets of 3-4 examples where all but exactly one example share a parity, yes-rate on non-member targets of the majority parity minus those of the minority parity; observed above null means people discount the odd-one-out example and keep the majority-parity rule more than the model's single inferred noise rate allows, below null means they discount it less.

results.name: shared_rule_count_effect
results.description: Among non-member targets, yes-rate for targets that satisfy >=2 of the simple rules (odd, even, multiples of 3/4/5/6/7/8/9, ends in d) shared by all examples minus yes-rate for targets satisfying exactly 1; observed above null means people demand conjunctive consistency (agreement with all shared regularities) more than the model's single-rule mixture, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: shared_rule_count_effect
# description: Among non-member targets, yes-rate for targets that satisfy >=2 of the simple rules (odd, even, multiples of 3/4/5/6/7/8/9, ends in d) shared by all examples minus yes-rate for targets satisfying exactly 1; observed above null means people demand conjunctive consistency (agreement with all shared regularities) more than the model's single-rule mixture, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    nums = np.arange(1, 101)
    rules = [nums % 2 == 1, nums % 2 == 0] + [nums % m == 0 for m in (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9)] + [nums % 10 == d for d in range(10)]
    R = np.array(rules)  # (rules, 100)
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    codes, inv = np.unique(sets, return_inverse=True)
    C = np.zeros((len(codes), 100), dtype=int)
    ISMEM = np.zeros((len(codes), 100), dtype=bool)
    for i, s in enumerate(codes):
        ex = np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) - 1
        shared = R[:, ex].all(axis=1)
        C[i] = R[shared].sum(axis=0)
        ISMEM[i, ex] = True
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy() - 1
    c = C[inv, t]
    nm = ~ISMEM[inv, t]
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    a, b = nm & (c >= 2), nm & (c == 1)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: lag1_same_set_autocorrelation
results.description: Pearson correlation between a trial's rating and the previous row's rating, over consecutive rows (trial_index increases by 1) with the same number_set; observed above null means sequential response perseveration/carry-over that the trial-independent model cannot produce, below null means alternation.

results.name: digit_position_transfer_rate
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that all end in the same digit d, the yes-rate on targets whose tens digit is d but which do not end in d (e.g. 64,94,84 -> 40-49); observed below null means the model over-generalises via its 'contains digit d' rules (people treat the shared digit as position-specific), observed above null means people transfer the digit across positions more than the model.

results.name: set_yes_rate_dispersion
results.description: Standard deviation across number_sets (those with >=20 trials) of the per-set yes-rate; observed above null means people differ between sets more than the model (model's set-level generalisation too uniform), observed below null means the model makes sets too different (people are more uniform across sets).

results.name: decade_match_effect
results.description: Among non-member targets 1-9 away from the nearest example, yes-rate when the target shares its decade (tens digit, 100 counted with 90s) with some example minus when it does not; observed above null means people use decade membership (an unmodelled 'in the 40s'-type concept) more than the model's distance-only intervals, below means less.
results.code:
# name: decade_match_effect
# description: Among non-member targets 1-9 away from the nearest example, yes-rate when the target shares its decade (tens digit, 100 counted with 90s) with some example minus when it does not; observed above null means people use decade membership (an unmodelled 'in the 40s'-type concept) more than the model's distance-only intervals, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    ex_arr = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    codes, inv = np.unique(sets.to_numpy(), return_inverse=True)
    M = np.full((len(codes), 4), -1000)
    for i, s in enumerate(codes):
        e = ex_arr[s]; M[i, :len(e)] = e
    E = M[inv]
    valid = E > -1000
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(E - t[:, None]), 10**6).min(axis=1)
    dec = lambda x: np.minimum(x // 10, 9)
    same = (valid & (dec(E) == dec(t)[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    base = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 9)
    a, b = base & same, base & ~same
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
